title: Cutaneous tuberculosis (scrofuloderma & others)
summary: Skin TB is uncommon in the UK but important: a cold neck abscess or sinus over a lymph node (scrofuloderma), a slowly spreading reddish-brown plaque (lupus vulgaris), or warty or nodular forms. Refer to TB services; treatment follows NICE NG33.

glance.think: A painless lump, sinus or scar over neck lymph nodes, or a chronic plaque, in someone from a high-incidence area or with TB contact.
glance.engine: *M. tuberculosis* reaching the skin from a deeper focus, by inoculation or by blood spread; tuberculids are immune reactions to TB elsewhere.
glance.backbone: Refer to the TB service for biopsy, culture and treatment (standard regimen, NICE NG33); screen contacts; test for HIV.
glance.never_miss: Pulmonary or disseminated TB, HIV co-infection, and drug interactions with rifampicin.

what: Skin infection by *Mycobacterium tuberculosis* complex (rarely *M. bovis* / BCG). Uncommon in the UK but seen in people from high-incidence countries, the immunosuppressed (HIV, anti-TNF, steroids), homeless people and those with prior TB contact. **Scrofuloderma** is the commonest form in many series: TB of an underlying structure (usually **cervical lymph node**, also bone/joint/epididymis) breaks through to the skin. Case 1 is a classic scrofuloderma with active pulmonary TB.
cause: Classify by **route** and **host immunity** (answer to the tutor's question):

head: Route
Form
Host immunity / bacillary load
rows: Naïve → multibacillary, becomes paucibacillary as immunity develops
Scrofuloderma: moderate/variable, multibacillary; periorificial: poor immunity, advanced internal TB
Acute **miliary** TB of skin; tuberculous gumma (metastatic abscess)
**Tuberculids**: papulonecrotic tuberculid, lichen scrofulosorum, erythema induratum (Bazin)
Strong immunity; TB focus elsewhere; PCR may detect DNA; resolve with anti-TB therapy

cause: **Mechanism in Case 1:** pulmonary TB → lymphatic spread to cervical nodes → caseating necrosis → cold abscess → direct (contiguous) extension through overlying dermis → nodules, ulcers, sinuses.

list: **Scrofuloderma:** firm, **painless**, initially skin-coloured then **dusky red/blue** subcutaneous nodules over the **neck** (submandibular, supraclavicular, anterior triangle), axilla, groin, chest wall; nodes **matted, non-tender** ("cold"). Nodules soften, discharge cheesy/watery material, form **undermined ulcers and sinus tracts**, healing slowly with **cord-like, puckered scars** and skin bridges.
Systemic: chronic cough, weight loss, night sweats, fever (Case 1).
**Lupus vulgaris:** slowly enlarging red-brown plaque on head/neck; diascopy shows **"apple-jelly" nodules**; scarring, tissue destruction; risk of SCC in long-standing lesions.
**TB verrucosa cutis:** warty plaque on hands, knees, buttocks.

**Tuberculids:** crops of necrotic papules on extensor limbs (papulonecrotic); tiny lichenoid follicular papules on trunk in children (lichen scrofulosorum); tender violaceous nodules on posterior calves of women that may ulcerate (erythema induratum).

Skin/node **biopsy**: caseating granulomas; **Ziehl–Neelsen** stain for AFB; **mycobacterial culture** (gold standard, weeks; gives drug sensitivity); **TB PCR / GeneXpert** (rapid, rifampicin resistance).
Node FNA/excision; sputum smear/culture (AFB+ in Case 1); **chest X-ray**.
**Mantoux / IGRA** support infection but do not separate latent from active disease (may be false-negative in HIV/miliary TB).
**HIV test** for every patient with TB (NICE NG33); also hepatitis B/C, LFTs, renal function, visual acuity (ethambutol) baselines.

head: Look-alike
Distinguishing clues
rows: Young child, unilateral submandibular node, violaceous skin, no lung disease; culture distinguishes
Jaw angle, "woody" induration, sinuses discharging **sulphur granules**
Axilla/groin, recurrent painful nodules, double-ended comedones, no systemic TB
Rubbery or hard nodes, B symptoms — biopsy
Acute, hot, tender, fluctuant, responds to drainage/antibiotics
Lupus vulgaris DDx: sarcoidosis, discoid lupus, leprosy

list: **Not managed in primary care** — refer **urgently** to the local **TB service** (respiratory/ID) and dermatology; suspected pulmonary TB with cough needs same-day advice and infection-control (mask, avoid waiting rooms).

Standard regimen (NICE NG33, specialist-initiated): **2 months RHZE** (rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) then **4 months RH** (longer for CNS/bone, drug resistance). Directly observed therapy where adherence risk. Pyridoxine with isoniazid in at-risk patients.
TB is a **notifiable disease** (the diagnosing clinician notifies UKHSA); **contact tracing** via the TB service.

red_flags: Cough, weight loss, night sweats or haemoptysis: urgent chest assessment.
Rifampicin is a strong enzyme inducer: review every interacting drug (contraceptives, anticoagulants, antiretrovirals).
pearls: **Interaction checker is essential:** rifampicin is a potent enzyme inducer — reduces efficacy of combined hormonal contraception (advise non-hormonal/IUD/medroxyprogesterone with adjustment per FSRH), warfarin/DOACs, antiretrovirals, antiepileptics, methadone, steroids, azoles. Orange urine/tears (stains soft contact lenses).
Hepatotoxicity (RHZ): counsel to report jaundice, dark urine, vomiting; avoid alcohol; LFT monitoring per specialist.
Ethambutol: report any visual change (colour vision) immediately.
A chronic painless neck lump/sinus, especially with cough, weight loss, or origin from a high-incidence country, is **TB until proven otherwise** — do not repeatedly treat with flucloxacillin.
Skin lesions heal with scarring; tuberculids clear only with anti-TB treatment of the hidden focus.
